How is it from extensiveness? Because of completely entrusting to the spiritual friends. How is it from individually observing reality? Because the benefited bodhisattvas generate the reality of rendering benefit to others. How is it from entering into complete knowledge? Because it brings about the complete knowledge that 'these are the benefits rendered by you other bodhisattvas.' By these very three, it should be known as from non-deterioration, from possessing compassion, and from being worthy of respect. For what purpose was it asked by the Elder Subhūti? By six causes: for the purpose of cutting off doubt, for the purpose of causing to enter into special aspiration, for the purpose of causing to enter subsequently into the profound meaning, for the purpose of non-reversal, for the purpose of generating intense joy, and for the purpose of the sublime Dharma remaining for a long time; it is the prajñāpāramitā for the purpose of the continuum of the lineage not being interrupted. In that regard, how do these not interrupt the lineage of the Buddha? For the purpose of cutting off the doubts of the doubtful; for the purpose of causing bodhisattvas whose continuums are not completely ripened and who desire merit to enter into special aspiration for the prajñāpāramitā from obtaining much merit; for the purpose of causing those whose continuums are completely ripened to enter into the profound meaning; for the purpose of those who are completely transformed not reversing due to obtaining much merit upon sustaining them; for the purpose of correctly generating joy in the very merit of realizing that Dharma by themselves for those of pure special resolve who have been benefited; and for the sake of the teaching of the Great Vehicle remaining for a long time in future times. In brief, it is for the purpose of correctly teaching the doubtful, for the purpose of causing bodhisattvas who desire merit and are completely ripened to correctly take it up, for the purpose of praising those who are completely transformed, and for the purpose of making those of pure special resolve correctly rejoice. The bodhisattvas are called sattva and mahāsattva because they are great by seven aspects of greatness. What are the seven greatnesses? The greatness of Dharma, mind, aspiration, resolve, accumulation, time, and going everywhere; whichever is appropriate for the stages of a bodhisattva.

ཅིའི་ཕྱིར་ཞེ་ན། བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའི་ཐེག་པ་ལ་ཡང་དག་པར་ཞུགས་པས་ཞེས་གསུངས་ཏེ། བྱང་ཆུབ་རྣམ་པ་གསུམ་ཉིད་ལས་ཁྱད་པར་དུ་འཕགས་པར་གྱུར་པ་གནས་བརྟན་རབ་འབྱོར་གྱིས་ཚུལ་བཞིན་དུ་དྲིས་པར་གྱུར་པ་ཡིན་ནོ། །ལེགས་སོ་བྱིན་ནས་བདག་གིས་སེམས་ཅན་ཇི་ཙམ་སེམས་ཅན་དུ་བསྡུ་བར་བསྡུས་པ་ཞེས་པས་ནི་སྤྱིའི་མཚན་ཉིད་བསྟན་པའོ། །སྒོ་ང་ལས་སྐྱེས་པའམ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་དེ་ལྟ་བུ་ལ་སོགས་པས་ནི་ཁྱད་པར་གྱི་མཚན་ཉིད་བསྟན་པ་སྟེ། དེ་ཡང་སྐྱེ་བ་དང་གནས་ཀྱི་ཁྱད་པར་སྨོས་པའི་དབྱེ་བ་ལས་རིག་པར་བྱ་སྟེ།སྒོ་ང་། མངལ། དྲོད་གཤེར། བརྫུས་པ་རྣམས་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་སྐྱེ་བའི་དབྱེ་བའོ། །གཟུགས་ཅན་ནམ་གཟུགས་མེད་པ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་གནས་ཀྱི་དབྱེ་བའོ། །འདུ་ཤེས་ཅན་ནམ་འདུ་ཤེས་མེད་པའམ། འདུ་ཤེས་མེད་འདུ་ཤེས་མེད་མིན་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་ཡུལ་འཛིན་པའི་དབྱེ་བའོ། །ཇི་ཙམ་སེམས་ཅན་གྱི་ཁམས་སུ་གདགས་པས་བཏགས་པ་ཞེས་པ་ནི་མཚན་ཉིད་རྣམ་པ་གཉིས་པོ་དེ་ཉིད་ཀྱི་གནས་སྐབས་ཀྱི་སེམས་ཅན་གྱི་ཁམས་སངས་རྒྱས་སུ་བཏགས་པ་ཉིད་ངེས་པར་བསྟན་ཏོ། །ཐམས་ཅད་ཡོངས་སུ་མྱ་ངན་ལས་བཟླའོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་ཅི་ནས་ནུས་པ་མེད་པའི་དོན་དུ་གཉེར་བ་ཡིན་ནོ། །རིགས་ལས་ནི་ཇི་སྐད་བཤད་པའི་སྒོ་ང་ལས་སྐྱེས་པ་ལ་སོགས་པའི་རིགས་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱི་དབང་དུ་བྱས་ནས་སོ་ཞེས་དགོངས་ཀྱི། གྲངས་ལས་ནི་མ་ཡིན་ནོ། །

Why is that? Because it is taught, "since one has correctly entered the vehicle of the bodhisattvas"; it was asked properly by the Elder Subhūti concerning what is eminently distinguished from the very three aspects of awakening. Having given approval, "however many sentient beings are included in the inclusion of sentient beings by me" teaches the general defining characteristic. "Or born from eggs" and so forth teaches the specific defining characteristic; moreover, that should be known from the categories stating the distinctions of birth and abode: "eggs, wombs, heat and moisture, and miraculous births" is the category of birth. "Possessing form or formless" is the category of abode. "Possessing perception or non-perceiving, or neither perceiving nor non-perceiving" is the category of apprehending objects. "However many are designated by the designation of the realm of sentient beings" definitively teaches the very designation as Buddha of the realm of sentient beings in the occasion of those very two aspects of defining characteristics. "All shall be passed completely beyond sorrow" pursues the purpose of not being powerless by any means. "From family" intends that it is done with regard to all families such as "born from eggs" and so forth as was explained, but it is not from number.

heading: སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་གདུང་རྒྱུན་མི་འཆད་པ་བསྟན་པ།
translation: "Even though immeasurable sentient beings are thus passed completely beyond sorrow" completely shows as immeasurable individually the families such as "born from eggs" and so forth; it intends that "not any sentient being at all becomes passed beyond sorrow." What is the reason for that saying "there is not any at all" if it is said that "they are completely passed beyond sorrow by the bodhisattva himself"? "If a perception of a sentient being occurs in a bodhisattva, he should not be called a bodhisattva." What is the intention? If a perception of others as sentient beings occurs in a bodhisattva, due to perceiving a self, he should not be called a bodhisattva; what is the intention of what is said, "whoever has a perception of a sentient being, or a perception of a living being, or a perception of a person"? For whoever has the perception apprehending an afflicted sentient being, living being, and person occur, the perception of a self in that self also occurs, and the perception of a sentient being in a sentient being also occurs; in a bodhisattva, because of the very fact of having abandoned the view of a self, those do not occur. Therefore, the intention of this is that the bodhisattva who aspires to the very equality of self and others due to being equivalent in the defining characteristic of conditioned phenomena does not possess the view apprehending a sentient being, a living being, and a person.

ཇི་ལྟར་རྒྱས་པ་ལས་ཤེ་ན། དགེ་བའི་བཤེས་གཉེན་རྣམས་ལ་ཡོངས་སུ་གཏོད་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །ཇི་ལྟར་ཆོས་ཉིད་ལ་སོ་སོར་དམིགས་པ་ལས་ཤེ་ན། ཕན་བཏགས་པའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་རྣམས་ཀྱིས་གཞན་ལ་ཕན་འདོགས་པར་བྱེད་པའི་ཆོས་ཉིད་སྐྱེད་པར་བྱེད་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །ཇི་ལྟར་ཀུན་ཤེས་པ་ལ་འཇུག་པས་ཤེ་ན། བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་གཞན་ཁྱེད་རྣམས་ཀྱིས་ཕན་བཏགས་པ་ནི་འདི་དག་གོ་ཞེས་ཀུན་ཤེས་པར་བྱེད་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །གསུམ་པོ་འདི་རྣམས་ཉིད་ཀྱིས་མི་ཉམས་པ་ལས་དང་། སྙིང་རྗེ་དང་ལྡན་པ་ལས་དང་། གུས་པར་བྱ་བ་དག་ལས་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་རྣམས་རིག་པར་བྱའོ། །ཅིའི་དོན་དུ་གནས་བརྟན་རབ་འབྱོར་གྱིས་དྲིས་པར་གྱུར་ཞེ་ན། རྒྱུ་དྲུག་རྣམས་ཀྱིས་ཏེ། ཐེ་ཚོམ་གཅོད་པར་བྱེད་པའི་དོན་དང་། ལྷག་པར་མོས་པ་ལ་གཞུག་པའི་དོན་དང་། ཟབ་པའི་དོན་ལ་རྗེས་སུ་གཞུག་པའི་དོན་དང་། མ་ལོག་པའི་དོན་དང་། རབ་ཏུ་དགའ་བ་སྐྱེད་པར་བྱེད་པའི་དོན་དང་། དམ་པའི་ཆོས་སུ་རིང་དུ་གནས་པ་ཉིད་ཀྱི་དོན་ཏེ། གདུང་རྒྱུན་མི་འཆད་པའི་དོན་དུ་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པའོ། །དེ་ལ་ཇི་ལྟར་ན་འདི་དག་གིས་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་གདུང་མི་འཆད་ཅེ་ན། ཐེ་ཚོམ་ཅན་རྣམས་ཀྱི་ཐེ་ཚོམ་གཅོད་པར་བྱེད་པའི་དོན་དང་། བསོད་ནམས་འདོད་པ་རྒྱུད་ཡོངས་སུ་མ་སྨིན་པའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་རྣམས་ནི་བསོད་ནམས་མང་པོ་ཉིད་ཐོབ་པ་ལས་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་ལ་ལྷག་པར་མོས་སུ་གཞུག་པའི་དོན་དང་། རྒྱུད་ཡོངས་སུ་སྨིན་པ་རྣམས་ཟབ་མོའི་དོན་ལ་གཞུག་པའི་དོན་དང་། ཡོངས་སུ་གྱུར་པ་རྣམས་དེ་དག་རྗེས་སུ་འཛིན་པ་ལ་བསོད་ནམས་མང་པོ་ཉིད་ཐོབ་པས་མ་ལོག་པའི་དོན་དང་། ཕན་བཏགས་པའི་ལྷག་པའི་བསམ་པ་དག་པ་རྣམས་ཀྱི་བདག་ཉིད་ཆོས་དེ་རྟོགས་པའི་བསོད་ནམས་ཉིད་ལ་དགའ་བ་ཡང་དག་པར་སྐྱེད་པའི་དོན་དང་། མ་འོངས་པའི་དུས་སུ་ཐེག་པ་ཆེན་པོའི་བསྟན་པ་ཡུན་རིང་དུ་གནས་པའི་ཆེད་དུའོ། །མདོར་བསྡུ་ན་ཐེ་ཚོམ་ཅན་རྣམས་ལ་ཡང་དག་པར་བསྟན་པའི་དོན་དང་བསོད་ནམས་འདོད་པ་ཡོངས་སུ་སྨིན་པའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་རྣམས་ཡང་དག་པར་ལེན་དུ་གཞུག་པའི་དོན་དང་། ཡོངས་སུ་གྱུར་པ་རྣམས་གཟེངས་བསྟོད་པའི་དོན་དང་། ལྷག་པའི་བསམ་པ་དག་པ་རྣམས་ཡང་དག་པར་རབ་ཏུ་དགའ་བར་བྱེད་པའི་དོན་དུའོ། །བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་རྣམས་ནི་ཆེན་པོ་ཉིད་རྣམ་པ་བདུན་གྱིས་ཆེ་བའི་ཕྱིར་སེམས་དཔའ་ཞེས་དང་སེམས་དཔའ་ཆེན་པོ་སྟེ། ཆེན་པོ་ཉིད་བདུན་པོ་གང་དག་ཅེ་ན། ཆོས་དང་། སེམས་དང་། མོས་པ་དང་། བསམ་པ་དང་། ཚོགས་དང་། དུས་དང་། ཀུན་དུ་འགྲོ་བ་ཆེན་པོ་ཉིད་དེ། བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའི་ས་རྣམས་ལ་ཅི་རིགས་པར་རོ། །

How is it from extensiveness? Because of completely entrusting to the spiritual friends. How is it from individually observing reality? Because the benefited bodhisattvas generate the reality of rendering benefit to others. How is it from entering into complete knowledge? Because it brings about the complete knowledge that 'these are the benefits rendered by you other bodhisattvas.' By these very three, it should be known as from non-deterioration, from possessing compassion, and from being worthy of respect. For what purpose was it asked by the Elder Subhūti? By six causes: for the purpose of cutting off doubt, for the purpose of causing to enter into special aspiration, for the purpose of causing to enter subsequently into the profound meaning, for the purpose of non-reversal, for the purpose of generating intense joy, and for the purpose of the sublime Dharma remaining for a long time; it is the prajñāpāramitā for the purpose of the continuum of the lineage not being interrupted. In that regard, how do these not interrupt the lineage of the Buddha? For the purpose of cutting off the doubts of the doubtful; for the purpose of causing bodhisattvas whose continuums are not completely ripened and who desire merit to enter into special aspiration for the prajñāpāramitā from obtaining much merit; for the purpose of causing those whose continuums are completely ripened to enter into the profound meaning; for the purpose of those who are completely transformed not reversing due to obtaining much merit upon sustaining them; for the purpose of correctly generating joy in the very merit of realizing that Dharma by themselves for those of pure special resolve who have been benefited; and for the sake of the teaching of the Great Vehicle remaining for a long time in future times. In brief, it is for the purpose of correctly teaching the doubtful, for the purpose of causing bodhisattvas who desire merit and are completely ripened to correctly take it up, for the purpose of praising those who are completely transformed, and for the purpose of making those of pure special resolve correctly rejoice. The bodhisattvas are called sattva and mahāsattva because they are great by seven aspects of greatness. What are the seven greatnesses? The greatness of Dharma, mind, aspiration, resolve, accumulation, time, and going everywhere; whichever is appropriate for the stages of a bodhisattva.

ཅིའི་ཕྱིར་ཞེ་ན། བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའི་ཐེག་པ་ལ་ཡང་དག་པར་ཞུགས་པས་ཞེས་གསུངས་ཏེ། བྱང་ཆུབ་རྣམ་པ་གསུམ་ཉིད་ལས་ཁྱད་པར་དུ་འཕགས་པར་གྱུར་པ་གནས་བརྟན་རབ་འབྱོར་གྱིས་ཚུལ་བཞིན་དུ་དྲིས་པར་གྱུར་པ་ཡིན་ནོ། །ལེགས་སོ་བྱིན་ནས་བདག་གིས་སེམས་ཅན་ཇི་ཙམ་སེམས་ཅན་དུ་བསྡུ་བར་བསྡུས་པ་ཞེས་པས་ནི་སྤྱིའི་མཚན་ཉིད་བསྟན་པའོ། །སྒོ་ང་ལས་སྐྱེས་པའམ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་དེ་ལྟ་བུ་ལ་སོགས་པས་ནི་ཁྱད་པར་གྱི་མཚན་ཉིད་བསྟན་པ་སྟེ། དེ་ཡང་སྐྱེ་བ་དང་གནས་ཀྱི་ཁྱད་པར་སྨོས་པའི་དབྱེ་བ་ལས་རིག་པར་བྱ་སྟེ།སྒོ་ང་། མངལ། དྲོད་གཤེར། བརྫུས་པ་རྣམས་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་སྐྱེ་བའི་དབྱེ་བའོ། །གཟུགས་ཅན་ནམ་གཟུགས་མེད་པ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་གནས་ཀྱི་དབྱེ་བའོ། །འདུ་ཤེས་ཅན་ནམ་འདུ་ཤེས་མེད་པའམ། འདུ་ཤེས་མེད་འདུ་ཤེས་མེད་མིན་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་ཡུལ་འཛིན་པའི་དབྱེ་བའོ། །ཇི་ཙམ་སེམས་ཅན་གྱི་ཁམས་སུ་གདགས་པས་བཏགས་པ་ཞེས་པ་ནི་མཚན་ཉིད་རྣམ་པ་གཉིས་པོ་དེ་ཉིད་ཀྱི་གནས་སྐབས་ཀྱི་སེམས་ཅན་གྱི་ཁམས་སངས་རྒྱས་སུ་བཏགས་པ་ཉིད་ངེས་པར་བསྟན་ཏོ། །ཐམས་ཅད་ཡོངས་སུ་མྱ་ངན་ལས་བཟླའོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་ཅི་ནས་ནུས་པ་མེད་པའི་དོན་དུ་གཉེར་བ་ཡིན་ནོ། །རིགས་ལས་ནི་ཇི་སྐད་བཤད་པའི་སྒོ་ང་ལས་སྐྱེས་པ་ལ་སོགས་པའི་རིགས་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱི་དབང་དུ་བྱས་ནས་སོ་ཞེས་དགོངས་ཀྱི། གྲངས་ལས་ནི་མ་ཡིན་ནོ། །

Why is that? Because it is taught, "since one has correctly entered the vehicle of the bodhisattvas"; it was asked properly by the Elder Subhūti concerning what is eminently distinguished from the very three aspects of awakening. Having given approval, "however many sentient beings are included in the inclusion of sentient beings by me" teaches the general defining characteristic. "Or born from eggs" and so forth teaches the specific defining characteristic; moreover, that should be known from the categories stating the distinctions of birth and abode: "eggs, wombs, heat and moisture, and miraculous births" is the category of birth. "Possessing form or formless" is the category of abode. "Possessing perception or non-perceiving, or neither perceiving nor non-perceiving" is the category of apprehending objects. "However many are designated by the designation of the realm of sentient beings" definitively teaches the very designation as Buddha of the realm of sentient beings in the occasion of those very two aspects of defining characteristics. "All shall be passed completely beyond sorrow" pursues the purpose of not being powerless by any means. "From family" intends that it is done with regard to all families such as "born from eggs" and so forth as was explained, but it is not from number.

Why is that? Because it is taught, "since one has correctly entered the vehicle of the bodhisattvas"; it was asked properly by the Elder Subhūti concerning what is eminently distinguished from the very three aspects of awakening. Having given approval, "however many sentient beings are included in the inclusion of sentient beings by me" teaches the general defining characteristic. "Or born from eggs" and so forth teaches the specific defining characteristic; moreover, that should be known from the categories stating the distinctions of birth and abode: "eggs, wombs, heat and moisture, and miraculous births" is the category of birth. "Possessing form or formless" is the category of abode. "Possessing perception or non-perceiving, or neither perceiving nor non-perceiving" is the category of apprehending objects. "However many are designated by the designation of the realm of sentient beings" definitively teaches the very designation as Buddha of the realm of sentient beings in the occasion of those very two aspects of defining characteristics. "All shall be passed completely beyond sorrow" pursues the purpose of not being powerless by any means. "From family" intends that it is done with regard to all families such as "born from eggs" and so forth as was explained, but it is not from number.

Likewise, because it is done with regard to those born from eggs or born from heat and moisture, and those possessing perception, non-perceiving, and neither perceiving nor non-perceiving, all sentient beings should by all means be applied to complete passing beyond sorrow by three causes: for the purpose of those born in unfree states going to a time of leisure, for the purpose of those born in leisure who are not completely ripened being completely ripened, and for the purpose of those who are completely ripened being liberated. From what? Because it is taught, "into the realm of passing beyond sorrow without remainder." It is the very saying, "there is no passing completely beyond sorrow." The Bhagavat has also taught passing beyond sorrow by way of enumerations, for the purpose of completely abandoning that of the first concentration and so forth. That is, even though they are disciplined by the buddhas with the aspect of a reflected human, the ultimate should also be attained. As to from what, "into the realm of passing beyond sorrow with remainder" was not taught. That is a common result, because it is the result of one's own previous karma and the instructions of the Buddha. Although not singularly final, [it is said] "from the very pervasion of suffering of embodied beings"; passing beyond sorrow with remainder is because it is the very result of human effort, because it is the very common result, and because it is the very ultimate. Even from the very result that is not thoroughly final, it is explained as exactly what is called "without remainder."

[2-6] translation already produced for this document:
"Even though immeasurable sentient beings are thus passed completely beyond sorrow" completely shows as immeasurable individually the families such as "born from eggs" and so forth; it intends that "not any sentient being at all becomes passed beyond sorrow." What is the reason for that saying "there is not any at all" if it is said that "they are completely passed beyond sorrow by the bodhisattva himself"? "If a perception of a sentient being occurs in a bodhisattva, he should not be called a bodhisattva." What is the intention? If a perception of others as sentient beings occurs in a bodhisattva, due to perceiving a self, he should not be called a bodhisattva; what is the intention of what is said, "whoever has a perception of a sentient being, or a perception of a living being, or a perception of a person"? For whoever has the perception apprehending an afflicted sentient being, living being, and person occur, the perception of a self in that self also occurs, and the perception of a sentient being in a sentient being also occurs; in a bodhisattva, because of the very fact of having abandoned the view of a self, those do not occur. Therefore, the intention of this is that the bodhisattva who aspires to the very equality of self and others due to being equivalent in the defining characteristic of conditioned phenomena does not possess the view apprehending a sentient being, a living being, and a person.

Why is that? Because it is taught, "since one has correctly entered the vehicle of the bodhisattvas"; it was asked properly by the Elder Subhūti concerning what is eminently distinguished from the very three aspects of awakening. Having given approval, "however many sentient beings are included in the inclusion of sentient beings by me" teaches the general defining characteristic. "Or born from eggs" and so forth teaches the specific defining characteristic; moreover, that should be known from the categories stating the distinctions of birth and abode: "eggs, wombs, heat and moisture, and miraculous births" is the category of birth. "Possessing form or formless" is the category of abode. "Possessing perception or non-perceiving, or neither perceiving nor non-perceiving" is the category of apprehending objects. "However many are designated by the designation of the realm of sentient beings" definitively teaches the very designation as Buddha of the realm of sentient beings in the occasion of those very two aspects of defining characteristics. "All shall be passed completely beyond sorrow" pursues the purpose of not being powerless by any means. "From family" intends that it is done with regard to all families such as "born from eggs" and so forth as was explained, but it is not from number.

Likewise, because it is done with regard to those born from eggs or born from heat and moisture, and those possessing perception, non-perceiving, and neither perceiving nor non-perceiving, all sentient beings should by all means be applied to complete passing beyond sorrow by three causes: for the purpose of those born in unfree states going to a time of leisure, for the purpose of those born in leisure who are not completely ripened being completely ripened, and for the purpose of those who are completely ripened being liberated. From what? Because it is taught, "into the realm of passing beyond sorrow without remainder." It is the very saying, "there is no passing completely beyond sorrow." The Bhagavat has also taught passing beyond sorrow by way of enumerations, for the purpose of completely abandoning that of the first concentration and so forth. That is, even though they are disciplined by the buddhas with the aspect of a reflected human, the ultimate should also be attained. As to from what, "into the realm of passing beyond sorrow with remainder" was not taught. That is a common result, because it is the result of one's own previous karma and the instructions of the Buddha. Although not singularly final, [it is said] "from the very pervasion of suffering of embodied beings"; passing beyond sorrow with remainder is because it is the very result of human effort, because it is the very common result, and because it is the very ultimate. Even from the very result that is not thoroughly final, it is explained as exactly what is called "without remainder."

"Even though immeasurable sentient beings are thus passed completely beyond sorrow" completely shows as immeasurable individually the families such as "born from eggs" and so forth; it intends that "not any sentient being at all becomes passed beyond sorrow." What is the reason for that saying "there is not any at all" if it is said that "they are completely passed beyond sorrow by the bodhisattva himself"? "If a perception of a sentient being occurs in a bodhisattva, he should not be called a bodhisattva." What is the intention? If a perception of others as sentient beings occurs in a bodhisattva, due to perceiving a self, he should not be called a bodhisattva; what is the intention of what is said, "whoever has a perception of a sentient being, or a perception of a living being, or a perception of a person"? For whoever has the perception apprehending an afflicted sentient being, living being, and person occur, the perception of a self in that self also occurs, and the perception of a sentient being in a sentient being also occurs; in a bodhisattva, because of the very fact of having abandoned the view of a self, those do not occur. Therefore, the intention of this is that the bodhisattva who aspires to the very equality of self and others due to being equivalent in the defining characteristic of conditioned phenomena does not possess the view apprehending a sentient being, a living being, and a person.

heading: རབ་ཏུ་སྦྱོར་བའི་མཚན་ཉིད་བསྟན་པ།
translation: By this saying, "if a perception of a sentient being occurs, or a perception of a living being occurs, or a perception of a person occurs, he should not be called a bodhisattva," how the mind should be thoroughly held at the time of overcoming distraction is completely taught. As for how a perception of a sentient being does not occur in a bodhisattva at the time of entering evenly into yoga or at the time of overcoming distraction, it is the state to be known by such a defining characteristic. Therefore, thinking "not any sentient being at all becomes completely passed beyond sorrow," these become two non-engagements in mind.

Likewise, because it is done with regard to those born from eggs or born from heat and moisture, and those possessing perception, non-perceiving, and neither perceiving nor non-perceiving, all sentient beings should by all means be applied to complete passing beyond sorrow by three causes: for the purpose of those born in unfree states going to a time of leisure, for the purpose of those born in leisure who are not completely ripened being completely ripened, and for the purpose of those who are completely ripened being liberated. From what? Because it is taught, "into the realm of passing beyond sorrow without remainder." It is the very saying, "there is no passing completely beyond sorrow." The Bhagavat has also taught passing beyond sorrow by way of enumerations, for the purpose of completely abandoning that of the first concentration and so forth. That is, even though they are disciplined by the buddhas with the aspect of a reflected human, the ultimate should also be attained. As to from what, "into the realm of passing beyond sorrow with remainder" was not taught. That is a common result, because it is the result of one's own previous karma and the instructions of the Buddha. Although not singularly final, [it is said] "from the very pervasion of suffering of embodied beings"; passing beyond sorrow with remainder is because it is the very result of human effort, because it is the very common result, and because it is the very ultimate. Even from the very result that is not thoroughly final, it is explained as exactly what is called "without remainder."

"Even though immeasurable sentient beings are thus passed completely beyond sorrow" completely shows as immeasurable individually the families such as "born from eggs" and so forth; it intends that "not any sentient being at all becomes passed beyond sorrow." What is the reason for that saying "there is not any at all" if it is said that "they are completely passed beyond sorrow by the bodhisattva himself"? "If a perception of a sentient being occurs in a bodhisattva, he should not be called a bodhisattva." What is the intention? If a perception of others as sentient beings occurs in a bodhisattva, due to perceiving a self, he should not be called a bodhisattva; what is the intention of what is said, "whoever has a perception of a sentient being, or a perception of a living being, or a perception of a person"? For whoever has the perception apprehending an afflicted sentient being, living being, and person occur, the perception of a self in that self also occurs, and the perception of a sentient being in a sentient being also occurs; in a bodhisattva, because of the very fact of having abandoned the view of a self, those do not occur. Therefore, the intention of this is that the bodhisattva who aspires to the very equality of self and others due to being equivalent in the defining characteristic of conditioned phenomena does not possess the view apprehending a sentient being, a living being, and a person.

heading: སེམས་བསྐྱེད་པའི་དབང་དུ་བྱས་པ།
translation: Aspiration, prayer, and so forth, which have already been explained, are the defining characteristic of thorough application upon the support of thoroughly holding. By saying, "in other supports, based on that very aspiration and prayer, it will definitely emerge," aspiration, prayer, and so forth are once again extensively taught. From these, it should be known that how one applies in those above supports by means of five aspects is completely explained: from the deterioration of meaning, from being completely renowned as mere characteristics, from making clear, from completely establishing, and from making perfectly seen. The deterioration of meaning is the discordant class of the support. The mere characteristic of that very support is from being completely renowned. By aspiration and prayer, it is from making clear. Of the ultimate, it is from completely establishing. Entering evenly into yoga and overcoming distraction are from perfectly demonstrating.

དེ་བཞིན་དུ་ཡང་སྒོ་ང་ལས་སྐྱེས་པའམ་དྲོད་གཤེར་ལས་སྐྱེས་པ་རྣམས་དང་། འདུ་ཤེས་ཅན་དང་། འདུ་ཤེས་མེད་པ་དང་། འདུ་ཤེས་མེད་འདུ་ཤེས་མེད་མིན་རྣམས་དབང་དུ་བྱས་པའི་ཕྱིར་ཅི་ནས་སེམས་ཅན་ཐམས་ཅད་ཡོངས་སུ་མྱ་ངན་ལས་འདས་པ་ལ་རྒྱུ་གསུམ་གྱིས་སྦྱར་བར་བྱ་སྟེ། མི་ཁོམ་པར་སྐྱེས་པ་རྣམས་དལ་བའི་དུས་སུ་འགྲོ་བའི་ཕྱིར་དང་། དལ་བར་སྐྱེས་པ་ཡོངས་སུ་མ་སྨིན་པ་རྣམས་ཡོངས་སུ་སྨིན་པར་བྱེད་པའི་ཕྱིར་དང་། ཡོངས་སུ་སྨིན་པ་རྣམས་གྲོལ་བར་བྱེད་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །ཅི་ལས་ཤེ་ན། ལྷག་མ་མེད་པའི་མྱ་ངན་ལས་འདས་པའི་དབྱིངས་སུའོ་ཞེས་གསུངས་པ་ཡིན་ནོ། །མྱ་ངན་ལས་བཟླ་བ་མེད་དོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ཉིད་དོ། བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་རྣམ་གྲངས་ཀྱིས་ཀྱང་མྱ་ངན་ལས་འདས་པར་གསུངས་ཏེ། བསམ་གཏན་དང་པོ་ལ་སོགས་པ་དེའི་ཡོངས་སུ་སྤོང་བའི་དོན་དུའོ། །དེ་ནི་གཟུགས་བརྙན་གྱི་མིའི་རྣམ་པས་སངས་རྒྱས་རྣམས་ཀྱིས་གདུལ་བྱས་ཀྱང་སྟེ། ཤིན་ཏུ་བ་ཡང་ཐོབ་པར་བྱའོ། །ཅི་ལས་ན་ལྷག་མ་དང་བཅས་པའི་མྱ་ངན་ལས་འདས་པའི་དབྱིངས་སུ་ཞེས་ནི་མ་གསུངས་སོ། །དེ་ནི་ཐུན་མོང་གི་འབྲས་བུ་སྟེ། རང་གི་སྔོན་གྱི་ལས་དང་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་མན་ངག་གི་འབྲས་བུ་ཡིན་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །གཅིག་ཏུ་མཐར་ཐུག་པ་མ་ཡིན་ཀྱང་ལུས་ཅན་སྡུག་བསྔལ་བའི་ཁྱབ་པར་ཉིད་ལས་སོ་ཞེས་མྱ་ངན་ལས་འདས་པ་ལྷག་མ་དང་བཅས་པ་ནི་སྐྱེས་བུ་བྱེད་པའི་འབྲས་བུ་ཡིན་པ་ཉིད་ཀྱི་ཕྱིར་དང་། ཐུན་མོང་གི་འབྲས་བུ་ཡིན་པ་ཉིད་ཀྱི་ཕྱིར་དང་། ཤིན་ཏུ་བ་ཡིན་པ་ཉིད་ཀྱི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །ཤིན་ཏུ་མཐར་ཐུག་པ་མ་ཡིན་པའི་འབྲས་བུ་ཉིད་ལས་ཀྱང་ལྷག་མ་མེད་པ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ཉིད་དུ་བཤད་དོ། །

Likewise, because it is done with regard to those born from eggs or born from heat and moisture, and those possessing perception, non-perceiving, and neither perceiving nor non-perceiving, all sentient beings should by all means be applied to complete passing beyond sorrow by three causes: for the purpose of those born in unfree states going to a time of leisure, for the purpose of those born in leisure who are not completely ripened being completely ripened, and for the purpose of those who are completely ripened being liberated. From what? Because it is taught, "into the realm of passing beyond sorrow without remainder." It is the very saying, "there is no passing completely beyond sorrow." The Bhagavat has also taught passing beyond sorrow by way of enumerations, for the purpose of completely abandoning that of the first concentration and so forth. That is, even though they are disciplined by the buddhas with the aspect of a reflected human, the ultimate should also be attained. As to from what, "into the realm of passing beyond sorrow with remainder" was not taught. That is a common result, because it is the result of one's own previous karma and the instructions of the Buddha. Although not singularly final, [it is said] "from the very pervasion of suffering of embodied beings"; passing beyond sorrow with remainder is because it is the very result of human effort, because it is the very common result, and because it is the very ultimate. Even from the very result that is not thoroughly final, it is explained as exactly what is called "without remainder."

"Even though immeasurable sentient beings are thus passed completely beyond sorrow" completely shows as immeasurable individually the families such as "born from eggs" and so forth; it intends that "not any sentient being at all becomes passed beyond sorrow." What is the reason for that saying "there is not any at all" if it is said that "they are completely passed beyond sorrow by the bodhisattva himself"? "If a perception of a sentient being occurs in a bodhisattva, he should not be called a bodhisattva." What is the intention? If a perception of others as sentient beings occurs in a bodhisattva, due to perceiving a self, he should not be called a bodhisattva; what is the intention of what is said, "whoever has a perception of a sentient being, or a perception of a living being, or a perception of a person"? For whoever has the perception apprehending an afflicted sentient being, living being, and person occur, the perception of a self in that self also occurs, and the perception of a sentient being in a sentient being also occurs; in a bodhisattva, because of the very fact of having abandoned the view of a self, those do not occur. Therefore, the intention of this is that the bodhisattva who aspires to the very equality of self and others due to being equivalent in the defining characteristic of conditioned phenomena does not possess the view apprehending a sentient being, a living being, and a person.

By this saying, "if a perception of a sentient being occurs, or a perception of a living being occurs, or a perception of a person occurs, he should not be called a bodhisattva," how the mind should be thoroughly held at the time of overcoming distraction is completely taught. As for how a perception of a sentient being does not occur in a bodhisattva at the time of entering evenly into yoga or at the time of overcoming distraction, it is the state to be known by such a defining characteristic. Therefore, thinking "not any sentient being at all becomes completely passed beyond sorrow," these become two non-engagements in mind.

heading: སེམས་བསྐྱེད་པའི་དབང་དུ་བྱས་པ།
translation: Therein, regarding the support of the completely pure pāramitās, as for whatever is taught first, saying "a bodhisattva gives a gift without abiding in things," its deterioration of meaning is what is taught, saying "the very abiding is the discordant class." As for whatever is taught, saying "gives a gift," that is from being completely renowned as mere characteristics.

དེ་བཞིན་དུ་ཡང་སྒོ་ང་ལས་སྐྱེས་པའམ་དྲོད་གཤེར་ལས་སྐྱེས་པ་རྣམས་དང་། འདུ་ཤེས་ཅན་དང་། འདུ་ཤེས་མེད་པ་དང་། འདུ་ཤེས་མེད་འདུ་ཤེས་མེད་མིན་རྣམས་དབང་དུ་བྱས་པའི་ཕྱིར་ཅི་ནས་སེམས་ཅན་ཐམས་ཅད་ཡོངས་སུ་མྱ་ངན་ལས་འདས་པ་ལ་རྒྱུ་གསུམ་གྱིས་སྦྱར་བར་བྱ་སྟེ། མི་ཁོམ་པར་སྐྱེས་པ་རྣམས་དལ་བའི་དུས་སུ་འགྲོ་བའི་ཕྱིར་དང་། དལ་བར་སྐྱེས་པ་ཡོངས་སུ་མ་སྨིན་པ་རྣམས་ཡོངས་སུ་སྨིན་པར་བྱེད་པའི་ཕྱིར་དང་། ཡོངས་སུ་སྨིན་པ་རྣམས་གྲོལ་བར་བྱེད་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །ཅི་ལས་ཤེ་ན། ལྷག་མ་མེད་པའི་མྱ་ངན་ལས་འདས་པའི་དབྱིངས་སུའོ་ཞེས་གསུངས་པ་ཡིན་ནོ། །མྱ་ངན་ལས་བཟླ་བ་མེད་དོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ཉིད་དོ། བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་རྣམ་གྲངས་ཀྱིས་ཀྱང་མྱ་ངན་ལས་འདས་པར་གསུངས་ཏེ། བསམ་གཏན་དང་པོ་ལ་སོགས་པ་དེའི་ཡོངས་སུ་སྤོང་བའི་དོན་དུའོ། །དེ་ནི་གཟུགས་བརྙན་གྱི་མིའི་རྣམ་པས་སངས་རྒྱས་རྣམས་ཀྱིས་གདུལ་བྱས་ཀྱང་སྟེ། ཤིན་ཏུ་བ་ཡང་ཐོབ་པར་བྱའོ། །ཅི་ལས་ན་ལྷག་མ་དང་བཅས་པའི་མྱ་ངན་ལས་འདས་པའི་དབྱིངས་སུ་ཞེས་ནི་མ་གསུངས་སོ། །དེ་ནི་ཐུན་མོང་གི་འབྲས་བུ་སྟེ། རང་གི་སྔོན་གྱི་ལས་དང་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་མན་ངག་གི་འབྲས་བུ་ཡིན་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །གཅིག་ཏུ་མཐར་ཐུག་པ་མ་ཡིན་ཀྱང་ལུས་ཅན་སྡུག་བསྔལ་བའི་ཁྱབ་པར་ཉིད་ལས་སོ་ཞེས་མྱ་ངན་ལས་འདས་པ་ལྷག་མ་དང་བཅས་པ་ནི་སྐྱེས་བུ་བྱེད་པའི་འབྲས་བུ་ཡིན་པ་ཉིད་ཀྱི་ཕྱིར་དང་། ཐུན་མོང་གི་འབྲས་བུ་ཡིན་པ་ཉིད་ཀྱི་ཕྱིར་དང་། ཤིན་ཏུ་བ་ཡིན་པ་ཉིད་ཀྱི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །ཤིན་ཏུ་མཐར་ཐུག་པ་མ་ཡིན་པའི་འབྲས་བུ་ཉིད་ལས་ཀྱང་ལྷག་མ་མེད་པ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ཉིད་དུ་བཤད་དོ། །
[2-5] translation already produced for this document:
Likewise, because it is done with regard to those born from eggs or born from heat and moisture, and those possessing perception, non-perceiving, and neither perceiving nor non-perceiving, all sentient beings should by all means be applied to complete passing beyond sorrow by three causes: for the purpose of those born in unfree states going to a time of leisure, for the purpose of those born in leisure who are not completely ripened being completely ripened, and for the purpose of those who are completely ripened being liberated. From what? Because it is taught, "into the realm of passing beyond sorrow without remainder." It is the very saying, "there is no passing completely beyond sorrow." The Bhagavat has also taught passing beyond sorrow by way of enumerations, for the purpose of completely abandoning that of the first concentration and so forth. That is, even though they are disciplined by the buddhas with the aspect of a reflected human, the ultimate should also be attained. As to from what, "into the realm of passing beyond sorrow with remainder" was not taught. That is a common result, because it is the result of one's own previous karma and the instructions of the Buddha. Although not singularly final, [it is said] "from the very pervasion of suffering of embodied beings"; passing beyond sorrow with remainder is because it is the very result of human effort, because it is the very common result, and because it is the very ultimate. Even from the very result that is not thoroughly final, it is explained as exactly what is called "without remainder."

དེ་ལྟར་སེམས་ཅན་ཚད་མེད་པ་ཡོངས་སུ་མྱ་ངན་ལས་བཟླས་ཀྱང་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་སྒོ་ང་ལས་སྐྱེས་པ་ལ་སོགས་པའི་རིགས་སོ་སོར་ཚད་མེད་པ་ཉིད་དུ་ཡོངས་སུ་སྟོན་ཏེ། སེམས་ཅན་འགའ་ཡང་མྱ་ངན་ལས་འདའ་བར་འགྱུར་བ་ནི་མ་ཡིན་ནོ་ཞེས་དགོངས་སོ། །བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་བདག་ཉིད་ཀྱིས་ཡོངས་སུ་མྱ་ངན་ལས་འདས་པར་གྱུར་ཞེས་བྱ་ན་འགའ་ཡང་མེད་དོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་དེ་ལ་གཏན་ཚིགས་ཅི་ཞེ་ན། གལ་ཏེ་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་སེམས་ཅན་དུ་འདུ་ཤེས་འཇུག་ན་དེ་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ཞེས་སྨྲ་བར་མི་བྱའོ། །དགོངས་པ་ཅི་ཡིན་ཞེ་ན། གལ་ཏེ་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་སེམས་ཅན་རྣམས་ལ་གཞན་དུ་འདུ་ཤེས་འཇུག་ན་བདག་ཏུ་འདུ་ཤེས་པས་དེ་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ཞེས་སྨྲ་བར་མི་བྱ་ལ། གང་སེམས་ཅན་དུ་འདུ་ཤེས་འཇུག་པའམ་སྲོག་ཏུ་འདུ་ཤེས་སམ་གང་ཟག་ཏུ་འདུ་ཤེས་ཞེས་བྱ་བའི་དགོངས་པ་ཅི་ཡིན་ཞེ་ན། གང་གི་ཉོན་མོངས་པ་ཅན་གྱི་སེམས་ཅན་དང་། སྲོག་དང་། གང་ཟག་ཏུ་འཛིན་པའི་འདུ་ཤེས་འཇུག་པ་དེའི་བདག་ལ་ཡང་བདག་ཏུ་འདུ་ཤེས་ཤིང་། སེམས་ཅན་ལ་ཡང་སེམས་ཅན་དུ་འདུ་ཤེས་འཇུག་སྟེ། བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ལ་ནི་བདག་ཏུ་ལྟ་བ་སྤངས་པ་ཉིད་ཀྱི་ཕྱིར་དེ་རྣམས་མི་འཇུག་གོ། །དེའི་ཕྱིར་འདུ་བྱེད་ཀྱི་མཚན་ཉིད་དུ་མཚུངས་པ་ཉིད་ཀྱིས་ན་བདག་དང་གཞན་མཉམ་པ་ཉིད་དུ་མོས་པ་གང་ཡིན་པའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་དེ་ནི་སེམས་ཅན་དང་། སྲོག་དང་། གང་ཟག་ཏུ་འཛིན་པའི་ལྟ་བ་ཅན་མ་ཡིན་ནོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་འདི་ནི་འདིའི་དགོངས་པ་ཡིན་ནོ། །

"Even though immeasurable sentient beings are thus passed completely beyond sorrow" completely shows as immeasurable individually the families such as "born from eggs" and so forth; it intends that "not any sentient being at all becomes passed beyond sorrow." What is the reason for that saying "there is not any at all" if it is said that "they are completely passed beyond sorrow by the bodhisattva himself"? "If a perception of a sentient being occurs in a bodhisattva, he should not be called a bodhisattva." What is the intention? If a perception of others as sentient beings occurs in a bodhisattva, due to perceiving a self, he should not be called a bodhisattva; what is the intention of what is said, "whoever has a perception of a sentient being, or a perception of a living being, or a perception of a person"? For whoever has the perception apprehending an afflicted sentient being, living being, and person occur, the perception of a self in that self also occurs, and the perception of a sentient being in a sentient being also occurs; in a bodhisattva, because of the very fact of having abandoned the view of a self, those do not occur. Therefore, the intention of this is that the bodhisattva who aspires to the very equality of self and others due to being equivalent in the defining characteristic of conditioned phenomena does not possess the view apprehending a sentient being, a living being, and a person.

དེ་ལྟར་སེམས་བསྐྱེད་པར་མི་བྱའོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་འདིས་ནི་ཇི་ལྟར་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔས་འདུན་པ་དང་སྨོན་ལམ་གྱིས་གནས་པར་བྱ་བ་དེ་ཡོངས་སུ་བསྟན་པ་ཡིན་ནོ། །

By this saying, "one should not generate the mind thus," how the bodhisattva should abide by aspiration and prayer is completely taught.

གལ་ཏེ་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་སེམས་ཅན་དུ་འདུ་ཤེས་འཇུག་ན་དེ་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ཞེས་མི་བྱ་བ་འདིས་ནི་རྣལ་འབྱོར་ལ་མཉམ་པར་གཞག་པའི་དུས་སུ་ཇི་ལྟར་བསྒྲུབ་པར་བྱ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་དེ་ཡོངས་སུ་བསྟན་ཏོ། །
[2-8] translation already produced for this document:

གང་སེམས་ཅན་དུ་འདུ་ཤེས་འཇུག་གམ། སྲོག་ཏུ་འདུ་ཤེས་འཇུག་གམ། གང་ཟག་ཏུ་འདུ་ཤེས་འཇུག་ན་དེ་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ཞེས་མི་བྱའོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་འདིས་ནི་རྣམ་པར་གཡེང་བ་ཚར་གཅོད་པའི་དུས་སུ་ཇི་ལྟར་སེམས་རབ་ཏུ་གཟུང་བར་བྱ་བ་དེ་ཡོངས་སུ་བསྟན་པ་ཡིན་ནོ། །ཇི་ལྟར་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་རྣལ་འབྱོར་ལ་སྙོམས་པར་འཇུག་པའི་དུས་སམ་རྣམ་པར་གཡེང་བ་ཚར་གཅོད་པའི་དུས་སུ་སེམས་ཅན་དུ་འདུ་ཤེས་པ་མི་འཇུག་ན་དེ་ལྟ་བུའི་མཚན་ཉིད་དེས་ཤེས་པར་བྱ་བའི་གནས་སྐབས་སོ། །དེའི་ཕྱིར་སེམས་ཅན་འགའ་ཡང་ཡོངས་སུ་མྱ་ངན་ལས་འདས་པར་འགྱུར་བ་མེད་དོ་སྙམ་དུ་འདི་དག་ཡིད་ལ་མི་བྱ་བ་གཉིས་སུ་འགྱུར་རོ། །
[2-9] translation already produced for this document:
By this saying, "if a perception of a sentient being occurs, or a perception of a living being occurs, or a perception of a person occurs, he should not be called a bodhisattva," how the mind should be thoroughly held at the time of overcoming distraction is completely taught. As for how a perception of a sentient being does not occur in a bodhisattva at the time of entering evenly into yoga or at the time of overcoming distraction, it is the state to be known by such a defining characteristic. Therefore, thinking "not any sentient being at all becomes completely passed beyond sorrow," these become two non-engagements in mind.

heading: ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་ལ་སྦྱོར་བའི་དབང་དུ་བྱས་པ།
source: འདིར་སྦྱིན་པའི་རང་བཞིན་གྱིས་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་དྲུག་པོ་ཐམས་ཅད་སྦྱིན་པ་རྣམ་པ་གསུམ་གྱི་དབང་དུ་བྱས་ནས་བསྡུས་པ་ཡིན་ཏེ། ཟང་ཟིང་གི་སྦྱིན་པས་ནི་སྦྱིན་པའི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པའོ། །མི་འཇིགས་པའི་སྦྱིན་པས་ནི་ཚུལ་ཁྲིམས་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་དང་། བཟོད་པའི་ཕ་ རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པའོ། །ཆོས་ཀྱི་སྦྱིན་པས་ནི་བརྩོན་འགྲུས་དང་། བསམ་གཏན་དང་། ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་སྟེ། བརྩོན་འགྲུས་མེད་ན་ཆོས་འཛིན་པ་དང་སྟོན་པ་ལ་སྐྱོ་བཞིན་པས་ཆོས་སྟོན་པར་མི་བྱེད་དོ། །བསམ་གཏན་མེད་ན་དད་པས་དབང་དུ་བྱ་བར་འདོད་པ་ཉིད་ཀྱིས་གྲང་བ་དང་ཚ་བ་མི་བཟོད་དེ། ཀུན་ནས་ཉོན་མོངས་པར་སྟོན་ཏོ། །ཤེས་རབ་མེད་ན་ཕྱིན་ཅི་ལོག་ཏུ་སྟོན་ཏེ་གང་ལས་ཉམས་པར་འགྱུར་ཞེས་བྱ་སྟེ། གསུམ་པོ་མེད་པ་མ་ཡིན་ན་ཆོས་ཀྱི་སྦྱིན་པ་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ་ཡིན་ནོ། །ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་དེ་རྣམས་ཀྱང་ཕ་རོལ་པ་དང་མཐོང་བའི་ཆོས་ཀྱི་འབྲས་བུ་རྣམ་པ་གཉིས་ཏེ། སྦྱིན་པའི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པས་ཕ་རོལ་གྱི་འབྲས་བུ་ལོངས་སྤྱོད་ཆེན་པོའོ། །ཚུལ་ཁྲིམས་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པས་བརྒྱ་བྱིན་ཉིད་དང་ཚངས་པ་ཉིད་ལ་སོགས་པའི་ལུས་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པའོ། །བཟོད་པའི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པས་ཕྱོགས་ཆེ་བ་དང་འཁོར་ཆེ་བའོ། །བརྩོན་འགྲུས་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པས་ནི་ལོངས་སྤྱོད་ལ་སོགས་པ་རྒྱུན་མི་འཆད་པའོ། །བསམ་གཏན་གྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པས་ནི་གནོད་པ་མེད་པ་སྒྲུབ་པོ། །ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པས་ནི་དབང་པོ་ཐམས་ཅད་རྣོ་ཞིང་བདེ་བ་དང་། ཡིད་བདེ་བ་མང་བ་དང་། སྐྱེ་བོའི་ཚོགས་ཆེན་པོ་ལ་དབང་སྒྱུར་བ་ཉིད་དོ། །མཐོང་བའི་ཆོས་ཀྱི་ནི་ཐམས་ཅད་ལྷག་པར་དད་པ་དང་། མཐོང་བའི་ཆོས་ལ་མྱ་ངན་ལས་འདས་པའོ། །དེ་ལ་གལ་ཏེ་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ཕ་རོལ་གྱི་སྦྱིན་པའི་འབྲས་བུ་དོན་དུ་གཉེར་བཞིན་པས་སྦྱིན་པ་ནི་དངོས་པོ་ལ་གནས་པས་སྦྱིན་པ་ཡིན་ཏེ། སྦྱིན་བྱའི་དངོས་པོ་དང་། དེ་ལྟ་བུའི་འབྲས་བུའི་དངོས་པོ་ལ་གནས་པ་ཉིད་ཀྱི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །
translation: Here, by the nature of generosity, all six pāramitās are included by way of the three kinds of generosity: by the generosity of material things, there is the pāramitā of generosity; by the generosity of fearlessness, there is the pāramitā of moral discipline and the pāramitā of patience; by the generosity of Dharma, there is the pāramitā of joyous effort, concentration, and wisdom. If there is no joyous effort, one does not teach the Dharma, being weary of holding and teaching the Dharma. If there is no concentration, due to the very desire to bring under control by faith, one does not endure cold and heat, and teaches in a completely afflicted manner. If there is no wisdom, one teaches erroneously, from which one will deteriorate. If one is not without the three, the generosity of Dharma is perfect. Those pāramitās also have two kinds of fruits: the future and seen phenomena. By the pāramitā of generosity, the future fruit is great wealth. By the pāramitā of moral discipline, there is a perfect body such as the very state of Śakra and the very state of Brahmā. By the pāramitā of patience, there is a great faction and a great retinue. By the pāramitā of joyous effort, wealth and so forth are uninterrupted. By the pāramitā of concentration, one accomplishes what is without harm. By the pāramitā of wisdom, all faculties are sharp and blissful, there is much mental bliss, and one has the very mastery over a great mass of people. As for those of seen phenomena, all are superior faith and passing beyond sorrow in seen phenomena. Therein, if a bodhisattva gives a gift while seeking the future fruit of generosity, the generosity is generosity by abiding in things, because of the very fact of abiding in the thing to be given and the thing of such a fruit.

[2-6] translation already produced for this document:
"Even though immeasurable sentient beings are thus passed completely beyond sorrow" completely shows as immeasurable individually the families such as "born from eggs" and so forth; it intends that "not any sentient being at all becomes passed beyond sorrow." What is the reason for that saying "there is not any at all" if it is said that "they are completely passed beyond sorrow by the bodhisattva himself"? "If a perception of a sentient being occurs in a bodhisattva, he should not be called a bodhisattva." What is the intention? If a perception of others as sentient beings occurs in a bodhisattva, due to perceiving a self, he should not be called a bodhisattva; what is the intention of what is said, "whoever has a perception of a sentient being, or a perception of a living being, or a perception of a person"? For whoever has the perception apprehending an afflicted sentient being, living being, and person occur, the perception of a self in that self also occurs, and the perception of a sentient being in a sentient being also occurs; in a bodhisattva, because of the very fact of having abandoned the view of a self, those do not occur. Therefore, the intention of this is that the bodhisattva who aspires to the very equality of self and others due to being equivalent in the defining characteristic of conditioned phenomena does not possess the view apprehending a sentient being, a living being, and a person.

གལ་ཏེ་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་སེམས་ཅན་དུ་འདུ་ཤེས་འཇུག་ན་དེ་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ཞེས་མི་བྱ་བ་འདིས་ནི་རྣལ་འབྱོར་ལ་མཉམ་པར་གཞག་པའི་དུས་སུ་ཇི་ལྟར་བསྒྲུབ་པར་བྱ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་དེ་ཡོངས་སུ་བསྟན་ཏོ། །

By this saying, "if a perception of a sentient being occurs in a bodhisattva, he should not be called a bodhisattva," how one should practice at the time of resting evenly in yoga is completely taught.

གང་སེམས་ཅན་དུ་འདུ་ཤེས་འཇུག་གམ། སྲོག་ཏུ་འདུ་ཤེས་འཇུག་གམ། གང་ཟག་ཏུ་འདུ་ཤེས་འཇུག་ན་དེ་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ཞེས་མི་བྱའོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་འདིས་ནི་རྣམ་པར་གཡེང་བ་ཚར་གཅོད་པའི་དུས་སུ་ཇི་ལྟར་སེམས་རབ་ཏུ་གཟུང་བར་བྱ་བ་དེ་ཡོངས་སུ་བསྟན་པ་ཡིན་ནོ། །ཇི་ལྟར་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་རྣལ་འབྱོར་ལ་སྙོམས་པར་འཇུག་པའི་དུས་སམ་རྣམ་པར་གཡེང་བ་ཚར་གཅོད་པའི་དུས་སུ་སེམས་ཅན་དུ་འདུ་ཤེས་པ་མི་འཇུག་ན་དེ་ལྟ་བུའི་མཚན་ཉིད་དེས་ཤེས་པར་བྱ་བའི་གནས་སྐབས་སོ། །དེའི་ཕྱིར་སེམས་ཅན་འགའ་ཡང་ཡོངས་སུ་མྱ་ངན་ལས་འདས་པར་འགྱུར་བ་མེད་དོ་སྙམ་དུ་འདི་དག་ཡིད་ལ་མི་བྱ་བ་གཉིས་སུ་འགྱུར་རོ། །
[2-9] translation already produced for this document:
By this saying, "if a perception of a sentient being occurs, or a perception of a living being occurs, or a perception of a person occurs, he should not be called a bodhisattva," how the mind should be thoroughly held at the time of overcoming distraction is completely taught. As for how a perception of a sentient being does not occur in a bodhisattva at the time of entering evenly into yoga or at the time of overcoming distraction, it is the state to be known by such a defining characteristic. Therefore, thinking "not any sentient being at all becomes completely passed beyond sorrow," these become two non-engagements in mind.

[2-10] source:
བཤད་ཟིན་པའི་འདུན་པ་དང་སྨོན་ལམ་ལ་སོགས་པ་ནི་ཡོངས་སུ་འཛིན་པའི་རྟེན་ལ་རབ་ཏུ་སྦྱོར་བའི་མཚན་ཉིད་དོ། །རྟེན་གཞན་རྣམས་སུ་དེ་ཉིད་འདུན་པ་དང་སྨོན་ལམ་ལ་བརྟེན་ནས་ངེས་པར་འབྱུང་བར་འགྱུར་རོ་ཞེས་འདུན་པ་དང་སྨོན་ལམ་ལ་སོགས་པ་སླར་ཡང་རྒྱས་པར་བསྟན་པ་ཡིན་ནོ། །འདི་དག་ལས་གོང་གི་རྟེན་དེ་རྣམས་སུ་རྣམ་པ་ལྔ་རྣམས་ཀྱིས་ཇི་ལྟར་སྦྱོར་བ་རྣམ་པར་བཤད་པར་རིག་པར་བྱ་སྟེ། དོན་ཉམས་པ་དང་། མཚན་མ་ཙམ་ཡོངས་སུ་གྲགས་པ་དང་། གསལ་བར་བྱེད་པ་དང་། རྣམ་པར་འཇོག་པར་བྱེད་པ་དང་། ཡང་དག་པར་མཐོང་བར་བྱེད་པ་ལས་སོ། །དོན་ཉམས་པ་ནི་རྟེན་གྱི་མི་མཐུན་པའི་ཕྱོགས་སོ། །རྟེན་དེ་ཉིད་ཀྱི་མཚན་མ་ཙམ་ནི་ཡོངས་སུ་གྲགས་པ་ལས་སོ། །འདུན་པ་དང་སྨོན་ལམ་གྱིས་ནི་གསལ་བར་བྱེད་པ་ལས་སོ། །དོན་དམ་པའི་ནི་རྣམ་པར་འཇོག་པར་བྱེད་པ་ལས་སོ། །རྣལ་འབྱོར་ལ་སྙོམས་པར་འཇུག་པ་དང་། རྣམ་པར་གཡེང་བ་ཚར་གཅོད་པ་དག་ནི་ཡང་དག་པར་སྟོན་པར་བྱེད་པ་ལས་སོ། །
[2-10] translation already produced for this document:
Aspiration, prayer, and so forth, which have already been explained, are the defining characteristic of thorough application upon the support of thoroughly holding. By saying, "in other supports, based on that very aspiration and prayer, it will definitely emerge," aspiration, prayer, and so forth are once again extensively taught. From these, it should be known that how one applies in those above supports by means of five aspects is completely explained: from the deterioration of meaning, from being completely renowned as mere characteristics, from making clear, from completely establishing, and from making perfectly seen. The deterioration of meaning is the discordant class of the support. The mere characteristic of that very support is from being completely renowned. By aspiration and prayer, it is from making clear. Of the ultimate, it is from completely establishing. Entering evenly into yoga and overcoming distraction are from perfectly demonstrating.

[2-11] source:
དེ་ལ་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་རྣམ་པར་དག་པའི་རྟེན་ལ་རེ་ཞིག་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔས་དངོས་པོ་ལ་མི་གནས་པར་སྦྱིན་པ་བྱིན་ནོ་ཞེས་གང་གསུངས་པ་ཡིན་ཏེ། དེའི་དོན་ཉམས་པ་ནི་གནས་པ་ཉིད་མི་མཐུན་པའི་ཕྱོགས་སོ་ཞེས་གསུངས་པ་ཡིན་ནོ། །སྦྱིན་པ་བྱིན་ནོ་ཞེས་གང་གསུངས་པ་དེ་ནི་མཚན་མ་ཙམ་ཡོངས་སུ་གྲགས་པ་ལས་སོ། །
[2-11] translation already produced for this document:
Therein, regarding the support of the completely pure pāramitās, as for whatever is taught first, saying "a bodhisattva gives a gift without abiding in things," its deterioration of meaning is what is taught, saying "the very abiding is the discordant class." As for whatever is taught, saying "gives a gift," that is from being completely renowned as mere characteristics.

heading: ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་ལ་སྦྱོར་བའི་དབང་དུ་བྱས་པ།
translation: Therefore, "gives a gift without abiding in things" is taught.

Work: འཕགས་པ་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་མ་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་རྡོ་རྗེ་གཅོད་པའི་དོན་བདུན་གྱི་རྒྱ་ཆེར་འགྲེལ་པ། (The Extensive Commentary on the Seven Points of the Noble Bhagavatī Mother Prajñāpāramitā Vajracchedikā), author: སློབ་དཔོན་དབྱིག་གཉེན།. A canonical Tibetan text; the blocks below are being translated in order.

Preceding blocks of this same document and their translations — match this terminology, register and line shape:

[2-6] source:
དེ་ལྟར་སེམས་ཅན་ཚད་མེད་པ་ཡོངས་སུ་མྱ་ངན་ལས་བཟླས་ཀྱང་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་སྒོ་ང་ལས་སྐྱེས་པ་ལ་སོགས་པའི་རིགས་སོ་སོར་ཚད་མེད་པ་ཉིད་དུ་ཡོངས་སུ་སྟོན་ཏེ། སེམས་ཅན་འགའ་ཡང་མྱ་ངན་ལས་འདའ་བར་འགྱུར་བ་ནི་མ་ཡིན་ནོ་ཞེས་དགོངས་སོ། །བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་བདག་ཉིད་ཀྱིས་ཡོངས་སུ་མྱ་ངན་ལས་འདས་པར་གྱུར་ཞེས་བྱ་ན་འགའ་ཡང་མེད་དོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་དེ་ལ་གཏན་ཚིགས་ཅི་ཞེ་ན། གལ་ཏེ་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་སེམས་ཅན་དུ་འདུ་ཤེས་འཇུག་ན་དེ་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ཞེས་སྨྲ་བར་མི་བྱའོ། །དགོངས་པ་ཅི་ཡིན་ཞེ་ན། གལ་ཏེ་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་སེམས་ཅན་རྣམས་ལ་གཞན་དུ་འདུ་ཤེས་འཇུག་ན་བདག་ཏུ་འདུ་ཤེས་པས་དེ་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ཞེས་སྨྲ་བར་མི་བྱ་ལ། གང་སེམས་ཅན་དུ་འདུ་ཤེས་འཇུག་པའམ་སྲོག་ཏུ་འདུ་ཤེས་སམ་གང་ཟག་ཏུ་འདུ་ཤེས་ཞེས་བྱ་བའི་དགོངས་པ་ཅི་ཡིན་ཞེ་ན། གང་གི་ཉོན་མོངས་པ་ཅན་གྱི་སེམས་ཅན་དང་། སྲོག་དང་། གང་ཟག་ཏུ་འཛིན་པའི་འདུ་ཤེས་འཇུག་པ་དེའི་བདག་ལ་ཡང་བདག་ཏུ་འདུ་ཤེས་ཤིང་། སེམས་ཅན་ལ་ཡང་སེམས་ཅན་དུ་འདུ་ཤེས་འཇུག་སྟེ། བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ལ་ནི་བདག་ཏུ་ལྟ་བ་སྤངས་པ་ཉིད་ཀྱི་ཕྱིར་དེ་རྣམས་མི་འཇུག་གོ། །དེའི་ཕྱིར་འདུ་བྱེད་ཀྱི་མཚན་ཉིད་དུ་མཚུངས་པ་ཉིད་ཀྱིས་ན་བདག་དང་གཞན་མཉམ་པ་ཉིད་དུ་མོས་པ་གང་ཡིན་པའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་དེ་ནི་སེམས་ཅན་དང་། སྲོག་དང་། གང་ཟག་ཏུ་འཛིན་པའི་ལྟ་བ་ཅན་མ་ཡིན་ནོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་འདི་ནི་འདིའི་དགོངས་པ་ཡིན་ནོ། །
[2-6] translation already produced for this document:
"Even though immeasurable sentient beings are thus passed completely beyond sorrow" completely shows as immeasurable individually the families such as "born from eggs" and so forth; it intends that "not any sentient being at all becomes passed beyond sorrow." What is the reason for that saying "there is not any at all" if it is said that "they are completely passed beyond sorrow by the bodhisattva himself"? "If a perception of a sentient being occurs in a bodhisattva, he should not be called a bodhisattva." What is the intention? If a perception of others as sentient beings occurs in a bodhisattva, due to perceiving a self, he should not be called a bodhisattva; what is the intention of what is said, "whoever has a perception of a sentient being, or a perception of a living being, or a perception of a person"? For whoever has the perception apprehending an afflicted sentient being, living being, and person occur, the perception of a self in that self also occurs, and the perception of a sentient being in a sentient being also occurs; in a bodhisattva, because of the very fact of having abandoned the view of a self, those do not occur. Therefore, the intention of this is that the bodhisattva who aspires to the very equality of self and others due to being equivalent in the defining characteristic of conditioned phenomena does not possess the view apprehending a sentient being, a living being, and a person.

[2-7] source:
དེ་ལྟར་སེམས་བསྐྱེད་པར་མི་བྱའོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་འདིས་ནི་ཇི་ལྟར་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔས་འདུན་པ་དང་སྨོན་ལམ་གྱིས་གནས་པར་བྱ་བ་དེ་ཡོངས་སུ་བསྟན་པ་ཡིན་ནོ། །
[2-7] translation already produced for this document:
By this saying, "one should not generate the mind thus," how the bodhisattva should abide by aspiration and prayer is completely taught.

[2-8] source:
གལ་ཏེ་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་སེམས་ཅན་དུ་འདུ་ཤེས་འཇུག་ན་དེ་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ཞེས་མི་བྱ་བ་འདིས་ནི་རྣལ་འབྱོར་ལ་མཉམ་པར་གཞག་པའི་དུས་སུ་ཇི་ལྟར་བསྒྲུབ་པར་བྱ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་དེ་ཡོངས་སུ་བསྟན་ཏོ། །
[2-8] translation already produced for this document:
By this saying, "if a perception of a sentient being occurs in a bodhisattva, he should not be called a bodhisattva," how one should practice at the time of resting evenly in yoga is completely taught.

[2-9] source:
གང་སེམས་ཅན་དུ་འདུ་ཤེས་འཇུག་གམ། སྲོག་ཏུ་འདུ་ཤེས་འཇུག་གམ། གང་ཟག་ཏུ་འདུ་ཤེས་འཇུག་ན་དེ་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ཞེས་མི་བྱའོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་འདིས་ནི་རྣམ་པར་གཡེང་བ་ཚར་གཅོད་པའི་དུས་སུ་ཇི་ལྟར་སེམས་རབ་ཏུ་གཟུང་བར་བྱ་བ་དེ་ཡོངས་སུ་བསྟན་པ་ཡིན་ནོ། །ཇི་ལྟར་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་རྣལ་འབྱོར་ལ་སྙོམས་པར་འཇུག་པའི་དུས་སམ་རྣམ་པར་གཡེང་བ་ཚར་གཅོད་པའི་དུས་སུ་སེམས་ཅན་དུ་འདུ་ཤེས་པ་མི་འཇུག་ན་དེ་ལྟ་བུའི་མཚན་ཉིད་དེས་ཤེས་པར་བྱ་བའི་གནས་སྐབས་སོ། །དེའི་ཕྱིར་སེམས་ཅན་འགའ་ཡང་ཡོངས་སུ་མྱ་ངན་ལས་འདས་པར་འགྱུར་བ་མེད་དོ་སྙམ་དུ་འདི་དག་ཡིད་ལ་མི་བྱ་བ་གཉིས་སུ་འགྱུར་རོ། །
[2-9] translation already produced for this document:
By this saying, "if a perception of a sentient being occurs, or a perception of a living being occurs, or a perception of a person occurs, he should not be called a bodhisattva," how the mind should be thoroughly held at the time of overcoming distraction is completely taught. As for how a perception of a sentient being does not occur in a bodhisattva at the time of entering evenly into yoga or at the time of overcoming distraction, it is the state to be known by such a defining characteristic. Therefore, thinking "not any sentient being at all becomes completely passed beyond sorrow," these become two non-engagements in mind.

[2-10] source:
བཤད་ཟིན་པའི་འདུན་པ་དང་སྨོན་ལམ་ལ་སོགས་པ་ནི་ཡོངས་སུ་འཛིན་པའི་རྟེན་ལ་རབ་ཏུ་སྦྱོར་བའི་མཚན་ཉིད་དོ། །རྟེན་གཞན་རྣམས་སུ་དེ་ཉིད་འདུན་པ་དང་སྨོན་ལམ་ལ་བརྟེན་ནས་ངེས་པར་འབྱུང་བར་འགྱུར་རོ་ཞེས་འདུན་པ་དང་སྨོན་ལམ་ལ་སོགས་པ་སླར་ཡང་རྒྱས་པར་བསྟན་པ་ཡིན་ནོ། །འདི་དག་ལས་གོང་གི་རྟེན་དེ་རྣམས་སུ་རྣམ་པ་ལྔ་རྣམས་ཀྱིས་ཇི་ལྟར་སྦྱོར་བ་རྣམ་པར་བཤད་པར་རིག་པར་བྱ་སྟེ། དོན་ཉམས་པ་དང་། མཚན་མ་ཙམ་ཡོངས་སུ་གྲགས་པ་དང་། གསལ་བར་བྱེད་པ་དང་། རྣམ་པར་འཇོག་པར་བྱེད་པ་དང་། ཡང་དག་པར་མཐོང་བར་བྱེད་པ་ལས་སོ། །དོན་ཉམས་པ་ནི་རྟེན་གྱི་མི་མཐུན་པའི་ཕྱོགས་སོ། །རྟེན་དེ་ཉིད་ཀྱི་མཚན་མ་ཙམ་ནི་ཡོངས་སུ་གྲགས་པ་ལས་སོ། །འདུན་པ་དང་སྨོན་ལམ་གྱིས་ནི་གསལ་བར་བྱེད་པ་ལས་སོ། །དོན་དམ་པའི་ནི་རྣམ་པར་འཇོག་པར་བྱེད་པ་ལས་སོ། །རྣལ་འབྱོར་ལ་སྙོམས་པར་འཇུག་པ་དང་། རྣམ་པར་གཡེང་བ་ཚར་གཅོད་པ་དག་ནི་ཡང་དག་པར་སྟོན་པར་བྱེད་པ་ལས་སོ། །
[2-10] translation already produced for this document:
Aspiration, prayer, and so forth, which have already been explained, are the defining characteristic of thorough application upon the support of thoroughly holding. By saying, "in other supports, based on that very aspiration and prayer, it will definitely emerge," aspiration, prayer, and so forth are once again extensively taught. From these, it should be known that how one applies in those above supports by means of five aspects is completely explained: from the deterioration of meaning, from being completely renowned as mere characteristics, from making clear, from completely establishing, and from making perfectly seen. The deterioration of meaning is the discordant class of the support. The mere characteristic of that very support is from being completely renowned. By aspiration and prayer, it is from making clear. Of the ultimate, it is from completely establishing. Entering evenly into yoga and overcoming distraction are from perfectly demonstrating.

[2-11] source:
དེ་ལ་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་རྣམ་པར་དག་པའི་རྟེན་ལ་རེ་ཞིག་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔས་དངོས་པོ་ལ་མི་གནས་པར་སྦྱིན་པ་བྱིན་ནོ་ཞེས་གང་གསུངས་པ་ཡིན་ཏེ། དེའི་དོན་ཉམས་པ་ནི་གནས་པ་ཉིད་མི་མཐུན་པའི་ཕྱོགས་སོ་ཞེས་གསུངས་པ་ཡིན་ནོ། །སྦྱིན་པ་བྱིན་ནོ་ཞེས་གང་གསུངས་པ་དེ་ནི་མཚན་མ་ཙམ་ཡོངས་སུ་གྲགས་པ་ལས་སོ། །
[2-11] translation already produced for this document:
Therein, regarding the support of the completely pure pāramitās, as for whatever is taught first, saying "a bodhisattva gives a gift without abiding in things," its deterioration of meaning is what is taught, saying "the very abiding is the discordant class." As for whatever is taught, saying "gives a gift," that is from being completely renowned as mere characteristics.

heading: ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་ལ་སྦྱོར་བའི་དབང་དུ་བྱས་པ།
translation: Alternatively, if one gives a gift while seeking the future fruits of moral discipline and so forth, it is generosity by abiding in something; therefore, "gives a gift without abiding in anything" is taught. Because there is no distinction in the very multiplicity of the fruits of moral discipline and so forth, the word "in anything" is stated.

"Even though immeasurable sentient beings are thus passed completely beyond sorrow" completely shows as immeasurable individually the families such as "born from eggs" and so forth; it intends that "not any sentient being at all becomes passed beyond sorrow." What is the reason for that saying "there is not any at all" if it is said that "they are completely passed beyond sorrow by the bodhisattva himself"? "If a perception of a sentient being occurs in a bodhisattva, he should not be called a bodhisattva." What is the intention? If a perception of others as sentient beings occurs in a bodhisattva, due to perceiving a self, he should not be called a bodhisattva; what is the intention of what is said, "whoever has a perception of a sentient being, or a perception of a living being, or a perception of a person"? For whoever has the perception apprehending an afflicted sentient being, living being, and person occur, the perception of a self in that self also occurs, and the perception of a sentient being in a sentient being also occurs; in a bodhisattva, because of the very fact of having abandoned the view of a self, those do not occur. Therefore, the intention of this is that the bodhisattva who aspires to the very equality of self and others due to being equivalent in the defining characteristic of conditioned phenomena does not possess the view apprehending a sentient being, a living being, and a person.

translation: Alternatively, if one gives while seeking the fruit of seen phenomena, bringing under control by faith, it is generosity by abiding in forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tactile objects; therefore, such things as "without abiding even in form" and so forth are taught. Alternatively, if one gives while seeking the passing beyond sorrow in seen phenomena, it is generosity by abiding in dharmas; therefore, "gives a gift without abiding even in dharmas" is taught. By this, whatever is taught exemplifying "a gift should be given," the aspiration and prayer for generosity are taught. As for whatever is taught saying "gives a gift without abiding," the very non-abiding is the complete establishment of the ultimate.

"Even though immeasurable sentient beings are thus passed completely beyond sorrow" completely shows as immeasurable individually the families such as "born from eggs" and so forth; it intends that "not any sentient being at all becomes passed beyond sorrow." What is the reason for that saying "there is not any at all" if it is said that "they are completely passed beyond sorrow by the bodhisattva himself"? "If a perception of a sentient being occurs in a bodhisattva, he should not be called a bodhisattva." What is the intention? If a perception of others as sentient beings occurs in a bodhisattva, due to perceiving a self, he should not be called a bodhisattva; what is the intention of what is said, "whoever has a perception of a sentient being, or a perception of a living being, or a perception of a person"? For whoever has the perception apprehending an afflicted sentient being, living being, and person occur, the perception of a self in that self also occurs, and the perception of a sentient being in a sentient being also occurs; in a bodhisattva, because of the very fact of having abandoned the view of a self, those do not occur. Therefore, the intention of this is that the bodhisattva who aspires to the very equality of self and others due to being equivalent in the defining characteristic of conditioned phenomena does not possess the view apprehending a sentient being, a living being, and a person.

By saying, "in other supports, based on that very aspiration and prayer, it will definitely emerge," aspiration, prayer, and so forth are once again extensively taught. heading: ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་ལ་སྦྱོར་བའི་དབང་དུ་བྱས་པ།
translation: Therein, by the very non-abiding, the ultimate to be meditated upon as it is is completely made clear, and by the very non-abiding in things and so forth, it is the very meditation on all that there is; it is whatever is taught saying, "how a bodhisattva gives a gift without abiding even in the perception of a characteristic." What is called "non-abiding" teaches the overcoming of distraction of one who has entered evenly into yoga, for at that time, there is no abiding in the perception of a characteristic.

"Even though immeasurable sentient beings are thus passed completely beyond sorrow" completely shows as immeasurable individually the families such as "born from eggs" and so forth; it intends that "not any sentient being at all becomes passed beyond sorrow." What is the reason for that saying "there is not any at all" if it is said that "they are completely passed beyond sorrow by the bodhisattva himself"? "If a perception of a sentient being occurs in a bodhisattva, he should not be called a bodhisattva." What is the intention? If a perception of others as sentient beings occurs in a bodhisattva, due to perceiving a self, he should not be called a bodhisattva; what is the intention of what is said, "whoever has a perception of a sentient being, or a perception of a living being, or a perception of a person"? For whoever has the perception apprehending an afflicted sentient being, living being, and person occur, the perception of a self in that self also occurs, and the perception of a sentient being in a sentient being also occurs; in a bodhisattva, because of the very fact of having abandoned the view of a self, those do not occur. Therefore, the intention of this is that the bodhisattva who aspires to the very equality of self and others due to being equivalent in the defining characteristic of conditioned phenomena does not possess the view apprehending a sentient being, a living being, and a person.

By saying, "in other supports, based on that very aspiration and prayer, it will definitely emerge," aspiration, prayer, and so forth are once again extensively taught. heading: ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་ལ་སྦྱོར་བའི་དབང་དུ་བྱས་པ།
translation: Thus, to some bodhisattva applying themselves to non-abiding, whether there is a lack of eagerness due to the very possessing of dependence on merit, or whether there is the aspect of seeking with eagerness, the very greatness of the heap of merit of giving a gift without abiding is completely taught; by three aspects, it is equal to space. By the very going everywhere, whether abiding or non-abiding, it is from being in accord with the arising of merit. By the very vastness, it is from the distinction of the supreme. By being inexhaustible, it is from limitless generosity.

[2-12] translation already produced for this document:
Here, by the nature of generosity, all six pāramitās are included by way of the three kinds of generosity: by the generosity of material things, there is the pāramitā of generosity; by the generosity of fearlessness, there is the pāramitā of moral discipline and the pāramitā of patience; by the generosity of Dharma, there is the pāramitā of joyous effort, concentration, and wisdom. If there is no joyous effort, one does not teach the Dharma, being weary of holding and teaching the Dharma. If there is no concentration, due to the very desire to bring under control by faith, one does not endure cold and heat, and teaches in a completely afflicted manner. If there is no wisdom, one teaches erroneously, from which one will deteriorate. If one is not without the three, the generosity of Dharma is perfect. Those pāramitās also have two kinds of fruits: the future and seen phenomena. By the pāramitā of generosity, the future fruit is great wealth. By the pāramitā of moral discipline, there is a perfect body such as the very state of Śakra and the very state of Brahmā. By the pāramitā of patience, there is a great faction and a great retinue. By the pāramitā of joyous effort, wealth and so forth are uninterrupted. By the pāramitā of concentration, one accomplishes what is without harm. By the pāramitā of wisdom, all faculties are sharp and blissful, there is much mental bliss, and one has the very mastery over a great mass of people. As for those of seen phenomena, all are superior faith and passing beyond sorrow in seen phenomena. Therein, if a bodhisattva gives a gift while seeking the future fruit of generosity, the generosity is generosity by abiding in things, because of the very fact of abiding in the thing to be given and the thing of such a fruit.

Alternatively, if one gives while seeking the fruit of seen phenomena, bringing under control by faith, it is generosity by abiding in forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tactile objects; therefore, such things as "without abiding even in form" and so forth are taught. Alternatively, if one gives while seeking the passing beyond sorrow in seen phenomena, it is generosity by abiding in dharmas; therefore, "gives a gift without abiding even in dharmas" is taught. By this, whatever is taught exemplifying "a gift should be given," the aspiration and prayer for generosity are taught. As for whatever is taught saying "gives a gift without abiding," the very non-abiding is the complete establishment of the ultimate.

translation: Again, as for the basis for the aspiration to attain the form body: regarding 'Subhūti, what do you think? Is the Tathāgata to be seen by the perfection of marks?', from the deterioration of meaning, it teaches that manifest pride in the Tathāgata with regard to the form body is the discordant class. If one is completely grasped by what kind of spiritual friend, if one asks by what kind, the elder Subhūti said, 'No.' The Bhagavan making it completely extensive is: 'Subhūti, however much there is perfection of marks, that much is false'; by this are the aspiration and prayer.

[2-12] translation already produced for this document:
Here, by the nature of generosity, all six pāramitās are included by way of the three kinds of generosity: by the generosity of material things, there is the pāramitā of generosity; by the generosity of fearlessness, there is the pāramitā of moral discipline and the pāramitā of patience; by the generosity of Dharma, there is the pāramitā of joyous effort, concentration, and wisdom. If there is no joyous effort, one does not teach the Dharma, being weary of holding and teaching the Dharma. If there is no concentration, due to the very desire to bring under control by faith, one does not endure cold and heat, and teaches in a completely afflicted manner. If there is no wisdom, one teaches erroneously, from which one will deteriorate. If one is not without the three, the generosity of Dharma is perfect. Those pāramitās also have two kinds of fruits: the future and seen phenomena. By the pāramitā of generosity, the future fruit is great wealth. By the pāramitā of moral discipline, there is a perfect body such as the very state of Śakra and the very state of Brahmā. By the pāramitā of patience, there is a great faction and a great retinue. By the pāramitā of joyous effort, wealth and so forth are uninterrupted. By the pāramitā of concentration, one accomplishes what is without harm. By the pāramitā of wisdom, all faculties are sharp and blissful, there is much mental bliss, and one has the very mastery over a great mass of people. As for those of seen phenomena, all are superior faith and passing beyond sorrow in seen phenomena. Therein, if a bodhisattva gives a gift while seeking the future fruit of generosity, the generosity is generosity by abiding in things, because of the very fact of abiding in the thing to be given and the thing of such a fruit.

[2-15] translation already produced for this document:
Alternatively, if one gives while seeking the fruit of seen phenomena, bringing under control by faith, it is generosity by abiding in forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tactile objects; therefore, such things as "without abiding even in form" and so forth are taught. Alternatively, if one gives while seeking the passing beyond sorrow in seen phenomena, it is generosity by abiding in dharmas; therefore, "gives a gift without abiding even in dharmas" is taught. By this, whatever is taught exemplifying "a gift should be given," the aspiration and prayer for generosity are taught. As for whatever is taught saying "gives a gift without abiding," the very non-abiding is the complete establishment of the ultimate.

Therein, by the very non-abiding, the ultimate to be meditated upon as it is is completely made clear, and by the very non-abiding in things and so forth, it is the very meditation on all that there is; it is whatever is taught saying, "how a bodhisattva gives a gift without abiding even in the perception of a characteristic." Here, by the nature of generosity, all six pāramitās are included by way of the three kinds of generosity: by the generosity of material things, there is the pāramitā of generosity; by the generosity of fearlessness, there is the pāramitā of moral discipline and the pāramitā of patience; by the generosity of Dharma, there is the pāramitā of joyous effort, concentration, and wisdom. If there is no joyous effort, one does not teach the Dharma, being weary of holding and teaching the Dharma. If there is no concentration, due to the very desire to bring under control by faith, one does not endure cold and heat, and teaches in a completely afflicted manner. If there is no wisdom, one teaches erroneously, from which one will deteriorate. If one is not without the three, the generosity of Dharma is perfect. Those pāramitās also have two kinds of fruits: the future and seen phenomena. By the pāramitā of generosity, the future fruit is great wealth. By the pāramitā of moral discipline, there is a perfect body such as the very state of Śakra and the very state of Brahmā. By the pāramitā of patience, there is a great faction and a great retinue. By the pāramitā of joyous effort, wealth and so forth are uninterrupted. By the pāramitā of concentration, one accomplishes what is without harm. By the pāramitā of wisdom, all faculties are sharp and blissful, there is much mental bliss, and one has the very mastery over a great mass of people. As for those of seen phenomena, all are superior faith and passing beyond sorrow in seen phenomena. Therein, if a bodhisattva gives a gift while seeking the future fruit of generosity, the generosity is generosity by abiding in things, because of the very fact of abiding in the thing to be given and the thing of such a fruit.

Alternatively, if one gives while seeking the passing beyond sorrow in seen phenomena, it is generosity by abiding in dharmas; therefore, "gives a gift without abiding even in dharmas" is taught. Here, by the nature of generosity, all six pāramitās are included by way of the three kinds of generosity: by the generosity of material things, there is the pāramitā of generosity; by the generosity of fearlessness, there is the pāramitā of moral discipline and the pāramitā of patience; by the generosity of Dharma, there is the pāramitā of joyous effort, concentration, and wisdom. If there is no joyous effort, one does not teach the Dharma, being weary of holding and teaching the Dharma. If there is no concentration, due to the very desire to bring under control by faith, one does not endure cold and heat, and teaches in a completely afflicted manner. If there is no wisdom, one teaches erroneously, from which one will deteriorate. If one is not without the three, the generosity of Dharma is perfect. Those pāramitās also have two kinds of fruits: the future and seen phenomena. By the pāramitā of generosity, the future fruit is great wealth. By the pāramitā of moral discipline, there is a perfect body such as the very state of Śakra and the very state of Brahmā. By the pāramitā of patience, there is a great faction and a great retinue. By the pāramitā of joyous effort, wealth and so forth are uninterrupted. By the pāramitā of concentration, one accomplishes what is without harm. By the pāramitā of wisdom, all faculties are sharp and blissful, there is much mental bliss, and one has the very mastery over a great mass of people. As for those of seen phenomena, all are superior faith and passing beyond sorrow in seen phenomena. Therein, if a bodhisattva gives a gift while seeking the future fruit of generosity, the generosity is generosity by abiding in things, because of the very fact of abiding in the thing to be given and the thing of such a fruit.

Alternatively, if one gives while seeking the fruit of seen phenomena, bringing under control by faith, it is generosity by abiding in forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tactile objects; therefore, such things as "without abiding even in form" and so forth are taught. Alternatively, if one gives while seeking the passing beyond sorrow in seen phenomena, it is generosity by abiding in dharmas; therefore, "gives a gift without abiding even in dharmas" is taught. By this, whatever is taught exemplifying "a gift should be given," the aspiration and prayer for generosity are taught. As for whatever is taught saying "gives a gift without abiding," the very non-abiding is the complete establishment of the ultimate.

Thus, to some bodhisattva applying themselves to non-abiding, whether there is a lack of eagerness due to the very possessing of dependence on merit, or whether there is the aspect of seeking with eagerness, the very greatness of the heap of merit of giving a gift without abiding is completely taught; by three aspects, it is equal to space. By the very going everywhere, whether abiding or non-abiding, it is from being in accord with the arising of merit. By the very vastness, it is from the distinction of the supreme. By being inexhaustible, it is from limitless generosity.

heading: གཟུགས་སྐུ་ཐོབ་པར་འདུན་པའི་དབང་དུ་བྱས་པ།
translation: Regarding the basis for the aspiration to attain the taught Dharma body: 'will there be any sentient beings who will generate such a perception?' is regarding 'the words at the end of a sūtra of such a mode.' Therein, 'the words of the sūtra' should be understood in the meaning of 'those that will be explained.' If one asks, 'In what kind of words?', they are whatever is taught as the words of the seven points. By the elder Subhūti, it is the very arising of bodhisattvas who generate the arising perception in the future time. Having refuted that they will not arise, the Bhagavan taught 'they will arise,' and the complete deterioration of practice during the destruction of the Dharma should also be known; if one asks, 'By what kind of practice in those?', by the total arising of what kind of cause, the form body of the Tathāgata is completely taught from completely proclaiming merely the cause of the perfection of marks, which is connected with 'by completely grasping merit.' That those possessing the perception by means of what kind of correct perception will arise is completely taught by the Bhagavan.

འདིར་སྦྱིན་པའི་རང་བཞིན་གྱིས་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་དྲུག་པོ་ཐམས་ཅད་སྦྱིན་པ་རྣམ་པ་གསུམ་གྱི་དབང་དུ་བྱས་ནས་བསྡུས་པ་ཡིན་ཏེ། ཟང་ཟིང་གི་སྦྱིན་པས་ནི་སྦྱིན་པའི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པའོ། །མི་འཇིགས་པའི་སྦྱིན་པས་ནི་ཚུལ་ཁྲིམས་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་དང་། བཟོད་པའི་ཕ་ རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པའོ། །ཆོས་ཀྱི་སྦྱིན་པས་ནི་བརྩོན་འགྲུས་དང་། བསམ་གཏན་དང་། ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་སྟེ། བརྩོན་འགྲུས་མེད་ན་ཆོས་འཛིན་པ་དང་སྟོན་པ་ལ་སྐྱོ་བཞིན་པས་ཆོས་སྟོན་པར་མི་བྱེད་དོ། །བསམ་གཏན་མེད་ན་དད་པས་དབང་དུ་བྱ་བར་འདོད་པ་ཉིད་ཀྱིས་གྲང་བ་དང་ཚ་བ་མི་བཟོད་དེ། ཀུན་ནས་ཉོན་མོངས་པར་སྟོན་ཏོ། །ཤེས་རབ་མེད་ན་ཕྱིན་ཅི་ལོག་ཏུ་སྟོན་ཏེ་གང་ལས་ཉམས་པར་འགྱུར་ཞེས་བྱ་སྟེ། གསུམ་པོ་མེད་པ་མ་ཡིན་ན་ཆོས་ཀྱི་སྦྱིན་པ་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ་ཡིན་ནོ། །ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་དེ་རྣམས་ཀྱང་ཕ་རོལ་པ་དང་མཐོང་བའི་ཆོས་ཀྱི་འབྲས་བུ་རྣམ་པ་གཉིས་ཏེ། སྦྱིན་པའི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པས་ཕ་རོལ་གྱི་འབྲས་བུ་ལོངས་སྤྱོད་ཆེན་པོའོ། །ཚུལ་ཁྲིམས་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པས་བརྒྱ་བྱིན་ཉིད་དང་ཚངས་པ་ཉིད་ལ་སོགས་པའི་ལུས་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པའོ། །བཟོད་པའི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པས་ཕྱོགས་ཆེ་བ་དང་འཁོར་ཆེ་བའོ། །བརྩོན་འགྲུས་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པས་ནི་ལོངས་སྤྱོད་ལ་སོགས་པ་རྒྱུན་མི་འཆད་པའོ། །བསམ་གཏན་གྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པས་ནི་གནོད་པ་མེད་པ་སྒྲུབ་པོ། །ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པས་ནི་དབང་པོ་ཐམས་ཅད་རྣོ་ཞིང་བདེ་བ་དང་། ཡིད་བདེ་བ་མང་བ་དང་། སྐྱེ་བོའི་ཚོགས་ཆེན་པོ་ལ་དབང་སྒྱུར་བ་ཉིད་དོ། །མཐོང་བའི་ཆོས་ཀྱི་ནི་ཐམས་ཅད་ལྷག་པར་དད་པ་དང་། མཐོང་བའི་ཆོས་ལ་མྱ་ངན་ལས་འདས་པའོ། །དེ་ལ་གལ་ཏེ་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ཕ་རོལ་གྱི་སྦྱིན་པའི་འབྲས་བུ་དོན་དུ་གཉེར་བཞིན་པས་སྦྱིན་པ་ནི་དངོས་པོ་ལ་གནས་པས་སྦྱིན་པ་ཡིན་ཏེ། སྦྱིན་བྱའི་དངོས་པོ་དང་། དེ་ལྟ་བུའི་འབྲས་བུའི་དངོས་པོ་ལ་གནས་པ་ཉིད་ཀྱི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །

Here, by the nature of generosity, all six pāramitās are included by way of the three kinds of generosity: by the generosity of material things, there is the pāramitā of generosity; by the generosity of fearlessness, there is the pāramitā of moral discipline and the pāramitā of patience; by the generosity of Dharma, there is the pāramitā of joyous effort, concentration, and wisdom. If there is no joyous effort, one does not teach the Dharma, being weary of holding and teaching the Dharma. If there is no concentration, due to the very desire to bring under control by faith, one does not endure cold and heat, and teaches in a completely afflicted manner. If there is no wisdom, one teaches erroneously, from which one will deteriorate. If one is not without the three, the generosity of Dharma is perfect. Those pāramitās also have two kinds of fruits: the future and seen phenomena. By the pāramitā of generosity, the future fruit is great wealth. By the pāramitā of moral discipline, there is a perfect body such as the very state of Śakra and the very state of Brahmā. By the pāramitā of patience, there is a great faction and a great retinue. By the pāramitā of joyous effort, wealth and so forth are uninterrupted. By the pāramitā of concentration, one accomplishes what is without harm. By the pāramitā of wisdom, all faculties are sharp and blissful, there is much mental bliss, and one has the very mastery over a great mass of people. As for those of seen phenomena, all are superior faith and passing beyond sorrow in seen phenomena. Therein, if a bodhisattva gives a gift while seeking the future fruit of generosity, the generosity is generosity by abiding in things, because of the very fact of abiding in the thing to be given and the thing of such a fruit.

Alternatively, if one gives while seeking the fruit of seen phenomena, bringing under control by faith, it is generosity by abiding in forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tactile objects; therefore, such things as "without abiding even in form" and so forth are taught. Alternatively, if one gives while seeking the passing beyond sorrow in seen phenomena, it is generosity by abiding in dharmas; therefore, "gives a gift without abiding even in dharmas" is taught. By this, whatever is taught exemplifying "a gift should be given," the aspiration and prayer for generosity are taught. As for whatever is taught saying "gives a gift without abiding," the very non-abiding is the complete establishment of the ultimate.

heading: གཟུགས་སྐུ་ཐོབ་པར་འདུན་པའི་དབང་དུ་བྱས་པ།
translation: By 'possessing moral discipline, possessing qualities, possessing wisdom,' the practice of the three trainings of superior moral discipline and so forth is completely taught, and the statement of qualities is the statement of concentration preceded by qualities such as having few desires. 'By them, reverence will be made to many hundreds of thousands of Buddhas' completely proclaims the total arising of the cause as being vast. Also, 'having extremely clear faith with a single mind' means generating the perception of those that arise at the very beginning from those which have just been explained. 'The Tathāgata knows them' means knowing their names, bodies, knowledge, and views by the Tathāgata.
